events.objective: Establish the true symptom onset and blast radius. Using logs and metrics, determine precisely when auth-service p99 latency and /v1/auth/login 503s began (minute-level), whether the degradation is only on the login endpoint or all auth-service endpoints, and whether other services in the login path (e.g. user-service, session-service, token/cache, DB) show correlated error/latency/resource anomalies over the same window. Report error signatures (timeouts, connection refused, crypto/CPU-related, OOM) and any CPU/memory/connection-pool trends on auth-service.

Find what changed and when, across ALL services, in the window before onset. Pull recent deployments and config changes (any service, not only auth-service), map auth-service's upstream/downstream dependencies for the login path, and check whether the reported bcrypt regression precedent matches this incident's signature (is it really the same failure mode?). Report concrete change timestamps and any shared components touched.

Test task b's candidate changes against the actual onset: for each deploy/config change identified in the login path, confirm whether auth-service latency/503 rate or the affected dependency's metrics step-changed at that timestamp (and did NOT change at other times). Also quantify whether auth-service CPU/resource usage is consistent with a bcrypt-style compute regression (CPU-bound, latency scaling with login volume) versus a downstream wait (idle/blocked threads, downstream latency).

events.statement: Across ALL services in 2026-04-18T00:00Z–2026-04-22T08:59Z there was exactly ONE deployment: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) deployed 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z by ci-bot, status live, not rolled back. No auth-service deployment of any kind is present.

The only config change in the window affecting auth-service is cfg-2801: key 'log.level', INFO→WARN, at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume'). This is a logging-verbosity change, not a functional/crypto parameter change.
No config changes were recorded for redis-cache in the same window (count 0).

auth-service login path dependencies: auth-service -> user-db (db), auth-service -> redis-cache (cache), auth-service -> kyc-provider (external), api-gateway -> auth-service (http). redis-cache is marked shared=true and user-db shared=false.

redis-cache is a SHARED component: it is a cache dependency of auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service. Notably portfolio-service — the one service that did deploy (2026-04-22T05:50Z) — shares redis-cache with auth-service.

The precedent cited in the report (HIST-101, 2025-08-14, 'Login latency after auth-service release', symptoms 'login p99 4s','503 on login','high cpu', root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', resolved by rolling back v6.4.0) is a bad_deployment whose signature requires an auth-service release. There is no auth-service release in the current window, so the same failure mode can be ruled out on change-history grounds.

events.answer: No auth-service deployment, config change, or release occurred in the window before onset — the only change touching auth-service was a log-level change (INFO→WARN) at 03:40Z, and the only deployment anywhere was portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z. The bcrypt-regression precedent (HIST-101) does not match this incident's signature: HIST-101 was caused by an auth-service *code release*, and no such release exists here. The login path depends on shared redis-cache and user-db; the plausible change vectors left are shared-component/infra changes rather than an auth-service deploy.

events.statement: auth-service p99 latency was flat at ~85-95 ms through 06:52:00Z, then jumped at the 06:54:00Z bucket to avg 3759.86 ms / max 3849.2 ms and stayed ~3.5-4.0s for the rest of the window.

auth-service CPU jumped from a ~33-40% baseline (06:00-06:45) to avg 84.31 / max 97.33 in the 06:50 bucket, and stayed ~96-98% through 08:50.

auth-service request_rate rose from a ~393-400 req/s baseline to avg 1078.03 / max 1813.74 in the 06:50 bucket, then settled ~1480-1520 req/s — roughly a 3.8x traffic surge at the same time as the CPU and latency jumps.
auth-service error_rate rose from ~0.2% baseline to avg 7.11 / max 14.76 in the 06:50 bucket, plateauing ~14% (HTTP 5xx) thereafter.
auth-service memory_pct stayed flat across the whole window (~51-55% avg, max 57.07), so the degradation is not memory/OOM-driven; the resource anomaly is CPU-only.

The deploy is not temporally coincident with the degradation.

redis-cache — the SHARED component that portfolio-service and auth-service both depend on (per F5) — shows no step change at the 05:50Z deploy nor at the 06:50-06:55Z auth onset: cpu_pct stays 21-22% flat across the entire 05:00-08:50 window (06:40 bucket avg 22.32, 06:50 bucket avg 21.57, 07:00 avg 22.14; summary min 19.51 max 25.59). No downstream cache resource anomaly exists to explain the auth degradation.

The auth-service onset is a simultaneous, single-bucket step at 06:50Z in BOTH load and saturation signals: request_rate jumps from ~390-395 req/s baseline (06:45 bucket avg 390.98) to avg 680.57/max 1012.36 in the 06:50 bucket, then 1475.5/max 1813.74 in the 06:55 bucket, settling ~1460-1540 req/s. auth-service CPU shows the identical 06:50 step (see next finding). Same timestamp, same bucket = coupled onset, and no other bucket in 05:00-08:59 shows a comparable discontinuity.

auth-service resource usage is consistent with a CPU-bound/compute-saturation regression, not a downstream wait: cpu_pct is flat at ~37-38% through 06:40 (06:40 bucket avg 38.46, max 40.45) then steps to avg 84.31/max 97.33 in the 06:50 bucket and pins at observed max 99.54 (06:50) / 98.84 (07:10) and sustains 96.7-97.7% avg for the rest of the window. A saturated-on-CPU service at ~97-98% with latency ~3.8s and no free capacity is the signature of compute-bound saturation, not of an idle/blocked thread pool waiting on a downstream.

auth-service self-throttling/rejection spikes in the SAME 06:50 bucket: rate_limited_per_min goes from ~1.7-2.2 req/min baseline (06:40 bucket avg 1.89) to avg 438.67/max 919.45 at 06:50, then plateaus ~890-915 req/min (avg 901.07 at 07:00; summary mean 469.4). The service is rejecting/limiting ~450x its baseline volume at the exact onset minute — an overload-saturation indicator on auth-service itself, not a downstream-induced wait.

No downstream-wait metric is available to support the 'downstream wait' hypothesis: redis-cache exposes only [connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct] — no latency metric; user-db exposes only [connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min] — no latency metric. So the login-path dependencies cannot present a latency-wait signature in this telemetry at all, which itself argues against a downstream-wait diagnosis being evidenced here; and no connection-pool/lag anomaly was observed in the metrics that DO exist (redis cpu flat).

events.answer: user-db and redis-cache both show NO degradation at the 06:50Z onset: user-db CPU (18%), slow queries (0.31/min) and replication lag (~30ms) are flat; its connections_active rises 25→75 from the 06:49 to 06:52 bucket, but that is an upward demand/connection-count step consistent with more clients arriving, not a slow/failing dependency (no CPU, no slow-query, no lag response), so it does not explain a downstream wait. redis-cache is healthy on every requested metric (hit ratio ~96%, clients ~309, evictions ~2.9/min, memory ~70.7%) with no step at 06:50Z. Conclusion: the previously incomplete basis for rejecting H2 is now funded — the downstreams show no step change at 06:50Z. H4 (capacity saturation) is supported: the only step at 06:50Z is on auth-service itself (load + CPU), and load propagates to user-db connections without any saturation appearing downstream.

events.statement: api-gateway request_rate is FLAT at ~1250 req/s from 05:00Z through 06:30Z (10/15-min buckets all avg 1237-1267), then steps up starting in the 06:45Z bucket (avg 2532.91, max 4859.74) and settles ~4875-4934 req/s from 07:00Z onward — a persistent ~3.9x elevation present at the gateway ingress itself, not just inside auth-service.

Zoomed to 120s buckets over 06:40-07:00Z, api-gateway request_rate climbs continuously from ~1266/1228 req/s (06:40/06:48) via 1500.82 (06:50) and 2327.7 (06:52) to 3294.15 (06:54), 3939.86 (06:56) and 4790.49 (06:58) — a smooth accelerating ramp, not a single hard step, agreeing in onset time with the auth-service surge (06:50Z).

api-gateway latency_p99_ms stays flat ~200-220 ms through the 06:51Z bucket (avg 207.77), then jumps to avg 3869.46 / max 4024.51 at 06:54Z and holds ~3.8-4.0s — showing the gateway only inherits the multi-second latency once upstream auth starts returning 503s, while the gateway volume ramp began ~1-2 buckets earlier.

api-gateway CPU is NOT saturated despite the ~3.9x traffic increase: cpu_pct stays flat at avg 36.9-44.9% across 06:40-07:10Z (e.g. 06:50 avg 40.93, 06:56 avg 43.39, mean 41.37). Unlike auth-service (which pins ~97-98%), the gateway has abundant headroom — the org-level episode is not gateway-side compute saturation.
auth-service restarts metric is exactly 0 for every 120s bucket across 06:40-07:00Z (min/max/mean all 0.0) — auth-service did NOT restart at or around the 06:50Z onset.

No api-gateway WARN-or-worse logs exist in 06:45-07:05Z (total_matched 0 across a data_range spanning 03:00-08:59Z) — the gateway emitted no load-shedding/throttling/error warnings of its own; its request_rate surge is not accompanied by any gateway-side rejection logging.

Interpretation: the ~3.8-3.9x request_rate surge is measured at api-gateway ingress too, so it is external/upstream of auth-service (real inbound load), not an auth-internal retry amplification or a metering artifact confined to auth-service. The gateway passes it through without saturating, while auth-service (which receives the same traffic) pins at ~97% CPU and begins 503-ing — consistent with H4 (auth-service capacity saturation), but the *origin* of the external load surge is not identified by these metrics.

tasks.objective: Establish the true symptom onset and blast radius. Using logs and metrics, determine precisely when auth-service p99 latency and /v1/auth/login 503s began (minute-level), whether the degradation is only on the login endpoint or all auth-service endpoints, and whether other services in the login path (e.g. user-service, session-service, token/cache, DB) show correlated error/latency/resource anomalies over the same window. Report error signatures (timeouts, connection refused, crypto/CPU-related, OOM) and any CPU/memory/connection-pool trends on auth-service.
tasks.answer: auth-service p99 latency and /v1/auth/login 503s both onset at ~06:52-06:54Z (before the 07:06 report). The degradation coincides with auth-service CPU pinning at ~97% and a request_rate surge from ~395 to ~1500 req/s; memory stayed flat, and all 372 error logs are "accept queue full ... 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)" — an overload/accept-queue symptom, not a crypto/OOM/timeout signature. Blast radius beyond auth-service could not be confirmed because dependency telemetry could not be queried (budget/known-service-name errors).

tasks.objective: Find what changed and when, across ALL services, in the window before onset. Pull recent deployments and config changes (any service, not only auth-service), map auth-service's upstream/downstream dependencies for the login path, and check whether the reported bcrypt regression precedent matches this incident's signature (is it really the same failure mode?). Report concrete change timestamps and any shared components touched.
tasks.answer: No auth-service deployment, config change, or release occurred in the window before onset — the only change touching auth-service was a log-level change (INFO→WARN) at 03:40Z, and the only deployment anywhere was portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z. The bcrypt-regression precedent (HIST-101) does not match this incident's signature: HIST-101 was caused by an auth-service *code release*, and no such release exists here. The login path depends on shared redis-cache and user-db; the plausible change vectors left are shared-component/infra changes rather than an auth-service deploy.

tasks.objective: Test task b's candidate changes against the actual onset: for each deploy/config change identified in the login path, confirm whether auth-service latency/503 rate or the affected dependency's metrics step-changed at that timestamp (and did NOT change at other times). Also quantify whether auth-service CPU/resource usage is consistent with a bcrypt-style compute regression (CPU-bound, latency scaling with login volume) versus a downstream wait (idle/blocked threads, downstream latency).
tasks.answer: Neither candidate change steps auth-service at its own timestamp: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (05:50Z) shows completely flat traffic/latency/cpu through the onset and redis-cache (the shared component it touches) is flat, so no change-history event lines up with the 06:50-06:55Z onset. The auth-service degradation is CPU-bound and self-inflicted: CPU pins at 97-98% while request_rate and rate_limited_per_min both jump ~3.8x and 450x respectively in the same 06:50 bucket, with no downstream latency, connection-pool, memory, or disk signal — consistent with a compute/saturation regression (or an abrupt inbound traffic surge), not a downstream wait, but NOT with a bcrypt-style code change since no auth-service deploy or config/crypto change exists in the window.

tasks.objective: Determine the provenance of the ~3.8x request_rate surge. Query api-gateway request_rate, latency_p99_ms, error_rate, and inbound request volume to auth-service over 06:40-07:00Z, plus auth-service 'restarts' over the same window. Did api-gateway inbound volume to auth-service rise ~3.8x at the 06:50Z bucket (external load), or is the surge absent upstream (implying internal retry/amplification or a metering artifact)? Also report whether auth-service restarted at onset. Do not re-issue failed queries for user-service logs; use available gateway/auth-service metrics.
tasks.answer: The ~3.8x surge is PRESENT UPSTREAM at the api-gateway, not absent: api-gateway request_rate rises from a flat ~1250 req/s baseline to ~4900 req/s (~3.9x) beginning at the 06:45-06:50Z bucket, alongside a matching latency jump. So the volume increase is real at ingress, not merely internal retry/amplification inside auth-service. However, the gateway itself does NOT saturate (CPU flat ~41%, zero WARN logs, near-zero errors until it merely reflects auth's 503s), and auth-service did NOT restart at onset (restarts metric = 0 throughout).

tasks.objective: Close the incomplete basis for rejecting H2 (downstream victim), using metrics that exist but were never queried. Fetch user-db metrics (connections_active, cpu_pct, slow_queries_per_min, replication_lag_ms) and redis-cache metrics (hit_ratio_pct, connected_clients, evictions_per_min, memory_pct) for 06:40-07:00Z, and report any step change at 06:50Z. Also check whether auth-service endpoints other than /v1/auth/login degraded in the same window (blast radius for H4). Avoid re-issuing known-failing queries (latency_p99_ms for redis-cache/user-db, thread_pool_active, user-service logs).
tasks.answer: user-db and redis-cache both show NO degradation at the 06:50Z onset: user-db CPU (18%), slow queries (0.31/min) and replication lag (~30ms) are flat; its connections_active rises 25→75 from the 06:49 to 06:52 bucket, but that is an upward demand/connection-count step consistent with more clients arriving, not a slow/failing dependency (no CPU, no slow-query, no lag response), so it does not explain a downstream wait. redis-cache is healthy on every requested metric (hit ratio ~96%, clients ~309, evictions ~2.9/min, memory ~70.7%) with no step at 06:50Z. Conclusion: the previously incomplete basis for rejecting H2 is now funded — the downstreams show no step change at 06:50Z. H4 (capacity saturation) is supported: the only step at 06:50Z is on auth-service itself (load + CPU), and load propagates to user-db connections without any saturation appearing downstream.

tasks.objective: Isolate H4 by ruling out a silent infra event elsewhere on the login path. Using ONLY metrics known to exist for those services: fetch available metrics for kyc-provider, kafka, and ledger-db/settlement over 06:40-07:05Z and report any step change at the 06:50-06:52Z bucket (use each service's exposed metrics; do not query latency_p99_ms on redis-cache/user-db, thread_pool_active, or user-service logs — these are known to fail). Also, using auth-service metrics (cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts), determine whether the degradation is confined to /v1/auth/login or present across all auth-service endpoints, and report the per-endpoint error/latency/rate-limit split over the onset window. Deliverable: a yes/no statement on whether any other login-path service step-changes at 06:50Z, plus the endpoint-breadth result.
tasks.answer: No — no other login-path service step-changes at the 06:50-06:52Z bucket: kafka cpu_pct/messages_in_per_s/under_replicated_partitions are flat (under-replicated=0 throughout), ledger-db cpu_pct is flat (06:50 avg 31.92), settlement-service cpu_pct is flat (06:50 avg 27.30); kyc-provider is an external dependency with no metrics at all, so it can only be judged via auth-service. Endpoint-breadth: I could NOT split by endpoint — see gaps.

critiques.summary: H4 is the correct leading hypothesis and is well-grounded on the auth-service side: load, CPU, latency, 5xx and self-throttling all step together in the single 06:50Z bucket (F9/F10/F15/F16/F17), memory is flat (F12), and the error signature is "accept queue full" (F8), not crypto/timeout/OOM. Alternatives are contradicted for H1 (no auth deploy, F1/F6) and H3 (no step at deploy time, F13; flat shared cache, F14). However two gaps prevent acceptance: (1) the 3.8x request_rate surge's provenance is unverified — if it is an internal retry/amplification artifact rather than external load, H4's stated chain (external surge → CPU saturation) rests on an assumption; (2) H2 (downstream victim) was rejected largely on absence of downstream anomalies, but user-db and redis-cache dashboards were never actually queried (only redis CPU was pulled). Both are cheap, obtainable, and could change ranking or trustworthiness. Cap confidence at 0.80.

challenges.issue: The causal chain's first hop ('3.8x surge is external/legitimate traffic or an upstream retry storm') is listed as an ASSUMPTION, not verified. No metric for api-gateway request rate/inbound traffic, nor auth-service restarts, was ever queried, so the origin of the surge is undetermined. If the surge is a metering/rate-limiter artifact or internal retry amplification, the stated chain is unsupported.

H2 was rejected on the ABSENCE of downstream anomalies, but the gaps admit user-db was fully unqueried and redis-cache was probed only on cpu_pct (hit_ratio, evictions, connected_clients never fetched). Rejecting a hypothesis from an incomplete result is a data-quality weakness; user-db connection-pool/replication-lag anomalies at 06:50Z are untested.

Onset coupling is established, but it is not verified whether the degradation is login-endpoint-only or affects all auth-service endpoints. This affects whether the cause is login-path-specific vs global capacity, though it does not overturn H4.

H1 ruled out on change-history (no auth deploy) and signature mismatch; this is solid, but the reason stated in some places leans on the rejecter treating 'no deploy feed entry' as conclusive. F1 covers the full window and is verified, so this is acceptable — noted only for rigor.

evidence_requests.rationale: Directly tests/eliminates H2 (downstream victim) using the metrics that DO exist but were never queried, closing the incomplete-result basis for its rejection; the endpoint check addresses blast radius for H4.

critiques.summary: Round 1's two blocking gaps are closed: T4 shows the ~3.9x surge is present at api-gateway ingress (F23/F24/F29), so it is genuinely upstream of auth-service rather than an internal retry/metering artifact; T5 and F19-F22 show user-db and redis-cache are flat on all exposed metrics across the 06:50Z onset, funding the rejection of H2. H1/H3/H5 remain contradicted on change-history and timing grounds (F1, F2, F6, F13, F14). H4 is therefore the correct origin and is well grounded end-to-end: coupled 06:50Z step in load+CPU (F9/F10/F15), CPU pinned 97-98% with flat memory (F16/F12), self-throttling ~450x (F17), CPU-bound error signature 'accept queue full' (F8), no restart (F27), gateway has headroom and its latency follows auth's 503s (F25/F26). Remaining limitation: the *provenance* of the external surge (legitimate traffic vs load test vs upstream retry from another caller) is not identified and is unmeasurable with existing telemetry (no caller-identity/route metric). This does not change the origin of the incident or the fix (auth-service capacity), so it is a confidence limiter and an explicit assumption, not a reason to keep spending rounds. Cap confidence at 0.85.

challenges.issue: Causal chain is verified on every hop except the one that H4 itself flags: the origin/driver of the ~3.8-3.9x inbound surge is unknown. F23/F24/F29 establish only that the surge exists upstream of auth-service (at gateway ingress), not what produced it. H4's statement ('real inbound load') is supported, but attribution to external demand vs a synthetic load test vs a retrying upstream caller is unproven and unmeasurable with the exposed metric set (no caller-identity/route metric). This is a/b a lower-confidence clause and an assumption, not a defect in the origin claim.

The binding-constraint assumption ('auth-service CPU allocation is fixed and is the ceiling') is inferred from the pin at ~97-98% (F16) because no provisioned-limit/allocatable-CPU metric exists. If the 06:50Z step were actually a capacity *reduction* (e.g. autoscaler min/allocatable change or node event), the mechanism would be a capacity change rather than pure demand growth — same fix, different trigger. No deploy/config evidence of such a change exists (F1, F2), so severity is low, but the inference is not direct.

H2 rests on a downstream-wait signature. F18/F22 show neither dependency exposes a latency metric, so 'downstream slow but not saturated' can only be shown unsupported, not excluded. F19-F21 (flat user-db cpu/slow_queries/lag, flat redis hit_ratio/evictions/clients/memory) plus the CPU-pinned/self-throttled auth signature (F16/F17) make a slow-not-saturated downstream an implausible residual, so this is non-blocking.

F1 covers deployments across all services for 2026-04-18..2026-04-22 08:59Z, but no auth-service release/deploy log was directly retrieved (open gap). RESOLVED for the decision: F1 is a verified, full-window all-services deployment observation, so the absence of an auth release is established; the missing log query is redundant confirmation, not blocking.

api-gateway has no per-route metric (open gap), so the gateway's aggregate ~3.9x surge is not proven to map 1:1 onto the auth-service login path. Magnitudes match (~3.9x vs ~3.8x) and onset times agree (F23/F24 vs F15), so the conclusion is unaffected, but the hop is inferred rather than measured.

evidence_requests.question: Over 06:40-07:05Z, did other services on the login path (kyc-provider, kafka, ledger-db/settlement) show any step change in their available metrics at the 06:50-06:52Z bucket, and is auth-service's degradation confined to /v1/auth/login or present across all its endpoints? Use only metrics known to exist for those services (auth-service exposes cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts).
evidence_requests.rationale: Closes the one remaining assumption that could support a different origin: a silent infra event (e.g. a redis/DNS/kafka failover like HIST-107) that never appears in the deploy/config feed would reopen H2/H4 discrimination. If nothing else on the login path steps at 06:50Z, H4's origin is fully isolated. Only request this if the metric budget allows and the metrics are known to exist for those services — do not re-issue known-failing queries (user-service logs, latency_p99_ms on redis-cache/user-db, thread_pool_active).

critiques.summary: H4 (capacity saturation of auth-service) is the correct top hypothesis and is grounded end-to-end on verified observations. Each causal hop rests on data, not assumption: the ~3.9x surge is measured at api-gateway ingress (F23/F24/F29), proving genuine upstream load rather than internal retry/metering; auth-service load and CPU step in the same 06:50Z bucket (F9/F10/F15), CPU pins at 97-98% with flat memory (F16/F12) and no restart (F27); self-throttling spikes ~450x (F17); the error signature is 'accept queue full ... 503' (F8) with errors lagging the queue build-up by ~2 buckets (F34); and api-gateway has ample headroom and only inherits latency once auth 503s (F25/F26/F28). Alternatives are contradicted by evidence, not dismissed: H1/H5 on change-history/timing (F1, F2, F6), H3 on no step at its own deploy timestamp plus flat shared cache (F13/F14), and H2 by directly measured flat downstream metrics at onset (F19-F22). All recent changes across all services were enumerated (F1). Residual uncertainty is confined to the *provenance* of the surge (no caller-identity/route metric exists — permanently unmeasurable) and per-endpoint blast radius, neither of which relocates the origin or changes the fix (auth-service capacity). Cap confidence at 0.85.

challenges.issue: The provenance of the ~3.8-3.9x inbound surge (legitimate demand vs synthetic load test vs an upstream caller retrying) is not identified. It does not change the origin (auth-service capacity is the binding constraint) or the fix, and no caller-identity/route metric exists in this telemetry, so it is an explicit assumption and a confidence limiter — not a reason to continue.

No direct provisioned-CPU-limit metric exists; saturation is inferred from the ~97-98% pin (F16). A capacity *reduction* at 06:50Z (autoscaler/node-allocatable event) was never directly checked and would imply the same fix with a different trigger. No deploy/config evidence of such a change exists (F1, F2), so this is a minor residual.

Per-endpoint blast radius within auth-service is unverified (the auth-service metric set has no endpoint dimension; F8 suggests confinement to /v1/auth/login but non-login endpoints were not measured). This is a secondary detail of an already-established origin, not a ranking or trustworthiness blocker.
